To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1) malaria was under-diagnosed in patients with a parasitaemia and 2) malaria was over-treated in patients with no parasitaemia.
in low malaria transmission settings, the clinical symptoms of malaria are unreliable and the use of microscopy to detect malaria is not feasible.
in low malaria transmission areas, the sensitivity and specificity of clinical signs and/or symptoms for the diagnosis of malaria are low.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the diagnosis of malaria in peripheral settings.
the diagnosis and treatment of malaria and the development and testing of new tools and strategies for malaria control.
the diagnosis of malaria in a low transmission area in south-western, Uganda.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the study has shown that in an area of relatively low malaria transmission in Uganda, the sensitivity of the clinical signs used by the health workers was poor and the specificity was very high, resulting in high rates of unnecessary treatment of malaria.
the study findings suggest that in areas of low transmission, malaria is a diagnosis of exclusion.
in areas of low transmission, the predictive values and positive and negative predictive values for clinical symptoms of malaria are poor.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
malaria case management is poor and that there is an urgent need to introduce rapid diagnostic tools to improve case management in this area.
the use of clinical signs and history alone is insufficient for accurate diagnosis of malaria in areas of low transmission.
in low transmission areas, the clinical signs and symptoms that have been used to diagnose malaria are poor predictors of malaria.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a need for more accurate and rapid diagnostic tools to improve the management of febrile diseases in low-transmission settings.

in low-transmission areas of Uganda, more than three-quarters of all febrile illnesses are not malaria, and the predictive value of the clinical signs used by health workers in diagnosing malaria is poor, and that a rapid, accurate and inexpensive diagnostic tool is needed for effective case management of malaria.

there is a need to develop a rapid diagnostic test which is cheap, simple, sensitive, and specific for malaria in low transmission settings, and to develop a diagnostic algorithm for the management of febrile illness in low transmission settings.
